content: Before the age of 18, many individuals experience sexual abuse. Both sexual violence and intimate partner violence are predominantly committed by men and boys against women and girls. However, men and boys, particularly younger boys, can also experience gender-based violence, though this is less common. Adolescent girls are especially vulnerable to sexual violence and abuse. Nearly one in four married or partnered adolescent girls aged 15–19 years are subjected to physical and/or sexual violence by their husband or partner. Intimate partner violence disproportionately affects adolescent girls in lowand lower-middle-income countries and regions. The differences in prevalence between highand lower-income regions are particularly stark for partner violence within the past year, likely due to challenges in leaving abusive relationships in resource-constrained settings and the high levels of stigmatization in these areas. Children with disabilities face nearly three times the risk of experiencing sexual violence compared to their non-disabled peers. For girls with disabilities, the highest risk occurs during adolescence. Adolescent girls with disabilities may also be subjected to forced sterilization, contraception, or abortion at the request of family members or healthcare professionals. These procedures are often justified under claims of medical necessity or best interest, but they are considered acts of violence under human rights frameworks. Girls with intellectual or psychosocial disabilities, particularly those living in residential institutions, are at the greatest risk of such violence. Sexual violence can lead to numerous physical and psychological burdens, including physical injuries, sexually transmitted infections (STIs), unintended pregnancies, emotional distress (such as fear, anger, self-blame, shame, sadness, or guilt), anxiety disorders (e.g., post-traumatic stress disorder), depression, medically unexplained somatic complaints, substance use disorders, and suicidal ideation or self-harm. Social trauma, including stigmatization, can result in social exclusion, discrimination, and rejection by family and community. Female genital mutilation (FGM) involves the partial or total removal of external genitalia or other injury to female genital organs for non-medical reasons. FGM has no health benefits and, instead, causes significant harm by interfering with the natural functioning of the body. It can lead to both immediate and long-term health consequences. FGM is most commonly performed on girls between birth and age 15 and is prevalent in 30 countries in Africa, as well as in parts of Asia and the Middle East. Due to international migration, the practice is now observed globally. Globally, 7 million adolescents aged 10–19 years were living with HIV in 2022, with adolescent girls accounting for 54% of the total. An estimated 140,000 adolescents were newly infected with HIV, three-quarters of whom were girls. Only about 65% of adolescents living with HIV were receiving antiretroviral therapy (ART) in 2022, compared to 77% ART coverage among adults aged 15 years and older. Factors such as age-disparate sexual relationships, low condom use, sexual violence, gender norms, and early sexual debut contribute to the disproportionate risk of HIV acquisition among adolescent females. In 2022, an estimated 27,000 adolescents worldwide died from AIDS-related causes, with East and Southern Africa recording the highest number of deaths (16,000 among those aged 10–19 years). Stigma, discrimination, punitive laws and policies, violence, and entrenched societal and gender inequalities continue to hinder access to HIV prevention and treatment for adolescents. The incidence of other STIs among adolescents was 7,089 per 100,000 population in 2019, with the highest rates among young adolescents aged 10–14 years. For example, the peak time for acquiring infections such as human papillomavirus (HPV) or herpes simplex virus-2 (HSV-2) is shortly after becoming sexually active, which typically occurs during adolescence. Communicable diseases remain a significant cause of adolescent mortality. In 2019, five of the top ten causes of death among adolescents were communicable diseases, including HIV/AIDS, diarrheal diseases, tuberculosis (TB), lower respiratory infections, and meningitis. Diarrheal diseases were the leading cause of death among young adolescent girls and the second leading cause among boys aged 10–14 years. Lower respiratory infections, such as influenza and pneumonia, were a major cause of adolescent deaths globally, particularly among younger adolescents. TB was the third leading cause of death among adolescents, with higher death rates among older adolescents and adolescent girls aged 15–19 years. Risk factors for TB include undernutrition, HIV infection, alcohol use, smoking, and diabetes. Mental health conditions are among the leading causes of illness and disability in adolescents. Anxiety disorders are the most common, characterized by excessive fear and worry, often accompanied by physical tension and behavioral or cognitive symptoms. Depression, or depressive disorder, involves prolonged periods of low mood or loss of interest in activities. Both anxiety and depression can interfere with daily life, family, social, and school functioning. Self-harm is a significant cause of death among adolescents, particularly older adolescents, and was the fourth leading cause of death in the 15–19 age group in 2019. The COVID-19 pandemic has likely exacerbated mental health challenges among adolescents, with increased rates of anxiety and depression reported during this period. Substance use, including alcohol and drugs, often begins during adolescence and is associated with a range of negative health and social consequences, such as accidents, violence, and risky behaviors. In 2016, more than one-quarter of adolescents aged 15–19 years were current drinkers, with males at higher risk of heavy episodic drinking. Physical inactivity is a widespread issue among adolescents, with 81% of those aged 11–17 years being insufficiently active in 2016. Regular physical activity provides numerous health benefits, including improved fitness, bone health, and psychosocial well-being. WHO recommends at least 60 minutes of moderate to vigorous physical activity daily for adolescents. Nutrition plays a crucial role in adolescent health. Malnutrition, whether due to undernutrition or obesity, and micronutrient deficiencies, such as iron deficiency anemia, are significant challenges. Iron deficiency anemia was a leading cause of adolescent morbidity in 2019, particularly in lowand middle-income countries. Overweight and obesity are also growing concerns, with more than one in six adolescents classified as overweight globally in 2016. Ensuring optimal nutrition during adolescence requires coordinated efforts across sectors, including health, education, and agriculture. Adolescents living in humanitarian and fragile settings face heightened health risks due to the breakdown of governance and health infrastructures. These settings often lead to increased mortality and morbidity among adolescents, who may take on adult responsibilities, such as caring for siblings or supporting their families. Vulnerable groups in these contexts include adolescents with disabilities, young adolescents, ethnic or religious minorities, child soldiers, young mothers, orphans, and survivors of sexual violence or trafficking.
